Jamaat, the Qawmi Establishment, and the Sunni Tradition in the Post-Revolution Politics of Power: An Impartial Analysis of Gains and Losses

## 1. The Post-Revolutionary Political Context

The post-revolutionary political phase of 2024 can be regarded as a *transitional political moment*, in which the breakdown of the existing power structure created opportunities for the emergence of new political configurations, alliances, and spheres of influence.

Historically, it has been observed that, during such periods, political forces that are well-organised, ideologically cohesive, and capable of formulating long-term strategies tend to benefit comparatively more.

Within this theoretical framework, different streams of Islamic politics have experienced gains and losses to varying degrees.

## 2. Jamaat-e-Islami: The Greatest Strategic Success

In this post-revolutionary reality, Jamaat-e-Islami has achieved the greatest strategic success.

According to the theory of *political opportunity structure*, the party has been able to make effective use of the changed circumstances.

From a comparatively weaker and defensive position in the past, it has transformed itself into a large, organised, and influential political force and moved closer to the centres of power.

Its ideological steadfastness, organisational discipline, and long-established cadre-based structure have provided it with a strategic advantage amid post-revolutionary uncertainty.

Consequently, its political risks are currently limited. If it succeeds in attaining state power, that will represent its greatest achievement. Even if such an opportunity does not materialise, establishing itself as a strong and effective opposition force will provide it with a lasting foundation in the politics of power in the future.

## 3. The Sunni Tradition: Reconstruction and Political Realignment

The post-revolutionary reconstruction of the Sunni tradition can be viewed as part of a process of social and political *realignment*.

Following a prolonged period of fragmentation and organisational weakness, it has reassessed its position and turned its attention towards internal unity and organisational consolidation.

In the language of social movement theory, this process of unification can be explained as *collective identity formation*.

If this continuity is maintained, the Sunni tradition may gradually emerge as an influential factor in national politics and become capable of playing a role in determining the balance of power.

## 4. The Qawmi Establishment: The Greatest Political Setback

On the other hand, in the context of post-revolutionary political transformation, the Qawmi establishment has emerged as the social and political force that has suffered the greatest losses.

From a theoretical perspective, this can be identified as a clear case of a *missed political opportunity*. According to social movement theory, any major political transformation creates a *“transformative moment”* for groups that actively participated in the movement. During this period, they may be able to convert their social influence and moral authority into institutional political capital.

For the Qawmi establishment, this possibility was both real and comparatively substantial. Considering its visible participation in the movement and its grassroots influence, it had a genuine opportunity to emerge as a distinct and organised force in national politics.

However, it failed to translate this potential into effective political capital. The expectation was that, during this post-revolutionary phase, the Qawmi establishment would develop a unified, institutional, and strategic framework and enter national politics with an independent political agenda.

The reality, however, has been different.

Due to internal divisions, a leadership crisis, and the absence of clear direction, it has gradually moved into a weaker position. The lack of effective leadership and the failure to ensure coordinated decision-making have obstructed its potential political transformation.

The immediate attraction of the politics of power, coupled with the absence of a long-term strategic vision, has pushed the Qawmi establishment towards multifaceted fragmentation. Instead of developing its own political distinctiveness and a collective position, it has sought shelter under the shadow of the major existing political forces and become divided into various parties and subgroups.

In this process, different segments have become engaged in mutual competition and conflict, further eroding their collective strength.

As a consequence, a significant segment of the Qawmi establishment has become confined within the two-sided power configuration centred around Jamaat and the BNP.

Within this framework, rather than developing an independent political identity and agenda, it has become a dependent and supportive force.

In the language of political sociology, this situation has seriously undermined both its *political autonomy* and its *competitive leverage*.

If this tendency gains institutional acceptance in the long run, the independent political identity of the Qawmi establishment will become even weaker, and the possibility of its returning to national politics as a strong, independent, and effective force will continue to diminish.
